General recipes
Here are some general recipes on which samples to use and how to use them. Given the complexity of Weak Boson processes (production, decay, multiplicity etc) and the
phase space you are interested in, there are no universal recipes that work for everyone. Feel free to contact via the mailing lists above if you have any questions.

Which samples/generators to use? For most commonly used weak boson processes, at least two MC generators are used to produce official samples: multi-leg
merged/matched samples (like Sherpa, MadGraph _aMC@NLO+Pythia8/Herwig) and inclusive samples (like PowhegBox, Herwig, VBFNLO, etc). If you are looking at
a phase space that is involved with high jet multiplicity, it's recommended to use the multi-leg MC samples.
Which processes to use? As for production mechanism, single-boson and diboson processes usually involve various production modes: quark-initiated, pure
electroweak production (vector-boson-fusion or vector-boson-scattering), and gluon-initiated (for diboson). Therefore, all different production modes should be
considered, and the relative contribution for each produciton mode could be quite different depending on the phase space. Care must be given to cases where Higgs
contribution should be included, since there could be overlap between weak boson samples and dedicated Higgs samples (for example, electroweak VVjj samples also
include VBF Higgs contribution). For detailed sample overlap, please refere to PmgWeakBosonProcesses#Overlap_with_Higgs_signal_sample and the detailed
description for each process below.
As for decay final states, one should also be careful when dealing with on-shell and off-shell contributions, since overlap could also happen between samples (for
example, electroweak VVjj samples and off-shell triboson VVV(->jj) samples could overlap).
Which cross-sections to use? Whenever possible, best SM predictions should be used, with high-order corrections (QCD and EW) included. The availability of high￾order corrections is highly dependent on the physics process. It is generally recommended to use the cross sections directly from AMI database or the
PmgCentralPage. There is also a tool available: PMGCrossSectionTool. Some details on the availability of high-order corrections can also be found below in
PmgWeakBosonProcesses#Higher_order_cross_sections. If you are able to get high-order corrections from some theorists, or calculate from some specific MC
generators, it is also justifiable to apply them in your analysis (assuming it is documented in detail somewhere and has been reviewed).
If you think the Central Page or AMI has an incorrect value for any of your samples, please report it following the instructions here.
Which systematic samples to use? Please refer to the recipes on systematic uncertainties below in PmgWeakBosonProcesses#Systematic_uncertainties.
Where the MC samples can be found? You can either find the detailed DSID for each weak boson process in the subsections below, or find them in the
PmgCentralPage. If you find any samples missing, please contact us! It could be that either the samples you are interested in exist but they are not listed, or simply
they don't exist.

V+jets Sherpa 2.2.1 For analyses using the baseline Sherpa 2.2.1 V+jets samples, the following sources of theoretical uncertainty should be considered: Scale variations: 7-point QCD scale variations stored as internal weights, from which the envelope around the nominal can be derived. The scale uncertainty is then given by the maximum shift of the envelope with respect to the nominal. Parton Density Function: The 100 NNPDF replicas can be passed through the LHAPDF tool as it has built-in methods to work out the combined PDF uncertainty, cf. PdfRecommendations. The central PDF values for the NNPDF3.0nnlo (PDF261000 or 303200 for the hessian method), MMHT2014nnlo68cl (PDF25300) and CT14nnlo (PDF13000) PDF sets are included as variations as well as two NNPDF3.0nnlo alpha_s variations (PDF269000 and PDF270000). CKKW and QSF variations: Parameterized V+jets uncertainties ( CDS ) are available and cover all scale variations including CKKW and QSF variations. Run AddZJetsWeights.py script (for both W+Jets and Z+jets) with the input file located at dev/SUSYTools here: /cvmfs/atlas.cern.ch/repo/sw/database/GroupData/dev/SUSYTools/Vjets_SysParameterization/VJetsWeights.root. The instruction can be found here. Some notes : Note: The PDF weights are missing in Sherpa 2.2.1 Zmumu samples.* These were produced before we figured out whether the production system would be able to handle>100 multi-weights. You can transfer the relative uncertainty that you get for Zee to Zmumu at the truth level (in the same fiducial phase-space). The collinear phase space is known to be mis-modeled with Sherpa (See M. Gignac's talk at BGF ). If your analysis is sensitive to this phase space, consider quoting additional uncertainty by comparing e.g. MadGraph vs Sherpa. It's a known issue that for Sherpa 2.2.1 V+jets samples, in some (rare) cases the nominal MC weights might be different from the weights corresponding to the trivial scale variation of "muF=1, muR=1" (see the example from the pt(Z) measurement). This is due to a (very rare) weight component coming from the parton shower that hasn’t been propagated through to the variations. When estimating systematic uncertainties, it's recommended to use the tool PMGSystematicsTool and PmgEventWeights. If it's not possible to use these PMG tools, it's recommended to work out the scale-uncertainty band with respect to the "muF=1, muR=1" variation and transfer the resulting uncertainty onto the prediction based on the nominal weight. Sherpa 2.2.11 For analyses using the new Sherpa 2.2.11 V+jets samples, the following sources of theoretical uncertainty should be considered: Scale variations 7-point QCD scale variations stored as internal weights in the baseline samples, from which the envelope around the nominal can be worked out. The scale uncertainty is then given by the maximum shift of the envelope with respect to the nominal. However, two versions of this scale variation exist: ME+PS: Coherent variation of the matrix element and parton shown renormalisation and factorisation QCD scales. (baseline recommendations for general physics analyses.) ME only: Variation of the matrix element renormalisation and factorisation QCD scales. (For special studies in case any analysis need the ME only impacts.) Parton Density Function The Hessian NNPDF3.0 NNLO uncertainty scheme is to be adopted, which can be accessed via the LHAPDF tool as it has built-in methods to work out the combined PDF uncertainty, cf. PdfRecommendations. The central PDF values for the NNPDF3.0nnlo (PDF261000), MMHT2014nnlo68cl (PDF25300) and CT14nnlo (PDF13000) PDF sets are included as variations as well as two NNPDF3.0nnlo alpha_s variations (PDF269000 and PDF270000). CKKW and QSF variations: Variation of the ME+PS merging/matching parameter (CKKW), and the resummation scale (QSF) are available as dedicated samples - see ATLMCPROD-9445 . The recommendation at present is to assess the systematics at EVNT-level via comparison to the baseline Sherpa 2.2.11 datasets. Known modelling issues
This page is work in progress!
Mismodelling in collinear V+jet topologies
Topologies where the boson gets close to a jet are not well modelled by the generators. For a systematic study of the mismodelling, see Matthew's presentation . In this
configuration, the boson represents the real-emission part of the NLO electroweak correction to QCD multijet production. It is not clear how much of the mismodelling can be
attributed to missing higher-order corrections.
Lepton eta asymmetry in Sherpa 2.2.1. V+jets
An asymmetry between the positive and negative part of the lepton-pseudorapidity distribution has been observed in all Sherpa 2.2.1 V+jets samples. The asymmetry has
been traced back to NLO-matched parton-shower emissions for non-trivial colour structures, such as V+2-jet NLO matrix elements. The bug only affects the 2-jet matrix
elements in this setup and is therefore mainly visible in such phase-space regions, where the effect is at the level of 2%.
The bug has been fixed as of Sherpa release 2.2.4. Currently there is no plan to release a general reweighting procedure for the existing samples, however if this problem
causes any particular issues in your analysis, please contact the FG+PMG convenors. Additional details are reported in this presentation at the PMG plenary .
Steps in B-filtered Sherpa 2.2.1 Z samples
Steps in the B-filtered Sherpa 2.2.1 samples have been observed in Z and b-jet <latex>p_\text{T}</latex> distributions. These effects are currently under investigation, and
have been discussed in a Focus Group meeting .
Normalisation discrepancies due to heavy-flavour-tags
Requiring one or more heavy-flavour tags can lead to normalisation differences on the order of 10-30% between data and simulation. This seems to be the case for all the
generators, see e.g. Section 5 in the boson+jets pub note or the studies collected on this livepage .

Treating pathological high-weight events in Sherpa samples
The Sherpa 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 samples contain rare events with very high weight magnitudes (|w|>100), in particular for processes with NLO accuracy in high-parton
multiplicities.
Technical explanation: These events correspond to phase space points with differential cross sections (weights) larger than the maximal weight estimated during the phase
space optimisation. To be completely consistent, during unweighting such events will always be accepted and have to be assigned a remainder weight of w=weight/maximum
to account for the imperfect MC integration.
These high (positive or negative) weights should only happen very rarely, and we basically keep these large weights only to allow for cross-checks that such instabilities don't
appear en masse in any particular sample or phase space region. If one such large weight creates a spike in your otherwise well populated distributions, it is fine to ignore it
by setting the weight to 1. If you see many such events entering your region of interest it's worth discussing this with PMG to understand whether the MC sample in question
would be expected to have problems there.
Note that these large event weights are being taken care of at the generator-level starting from v2.2.4 and so the prescription outlined above should no longer be necessary
for Sherpa samples using v2.2.4 or later.
